contents.subheaderText: A tool for Simple, Accessible, and Transferable Christian discipleship

contents: This section is meant to set the stage for everything that follows by addressing three core questions: Why discipleship matters, what discipleship actually is, and what it will require of you.
Before talking about methods or content, it is important to understand the answer to these questions.

contents: Discipleship shapes more than knowledge. It influences spiritual growth, relationships, and long-term faithfulness.
Growth happens most often when faith is practiced, discussed, and lived out with others.
Discipleship fosters deeper relationships marked by honesty, encouragement, and accountability.
As growth happens, faith is exercised through action and obedience.
Multiplying faith through others allows God's work to continue in and through others.

contents: A disciple is someone who learns how to grow, live, and express the Christian life and then repeats that process with others.
— Chasing Infinity, Mark Liederbach
Discipleship is the process of one person helping another live out that reality.
Discipleship includes four main elements:
Growing in relationship with God through the Bible and prayer.
Growing in faith is not a solitary experience. Other believers help provide encouragement, perspective, and accountability, especially in areas that are easy to overlook alone.
Each person has a unique environment. Classes, clubs, teams, and campus relationships provide opportunities for you to live out and share your faith with people you are uniquely able to reach.
Discipleship involves investing in others so they can invest in others, allowing faith to continue across generations.

contents: Discipleship is simple, but it requires intention and consistency.

contents: Transferable Discipleship is a tool designed to help followers of Jesus engage in discipleship that is simple, accessible, and transferable, providing a solid foundation for the journey of faith.
Jesus' command, "Go and make disciples…" (Matthew 28:19), is a mandate for all believers. We were created to make disciples.

contents.text: When you hear the phrase "make disciples," what comes to mind based on your past experiences?

contents: Biblical discipleship is not just about passing along good information. It is about seeing faithfulness and maturity continue from one generation to the next, building the same solid foundation in ways that others can then pass on.
Transferable Discipleship exists to help make that possible by keeping discipleship simple, accessible, and transferable.

contents.text: Why do you think discipleship often stops with one person instead of continuing to others?

contents: The content is structured in an easy-to-lead format, making it approachable for anyone. Each section is designed to be read together and to naturally spark meaningful discussion, not require expert knowledge or special training.
Discipleship resources can be difficult to find, and even harder to share once the person you have discipled begins discipling someone else. This app removes that barrier.
Transferable Discipleship is free and available to everyone. No cost. No searching. No barriers to entry.

Jesus spent three years discipling a small group of ordinary men, and then sent them out to change the world. They did not keep what He taught and modeled to themselves, and they did not wait until they had everything figured out before helping others.

contents.text: Which of the three values stands out most to you right now: simple, accessible, or transferable? Why?

contents: This material is not all-inclusive, but it focuses on essential concepts that lay a solid foundation for following Jesus. It is intentionally designed for quick replication, so that after completing these core concepts, anyone should feel prepared to begin discipling someone else.

contents.headerText: How does our sin separate us from God?
contents: Broken trust creates distance in any relationship. Without reconciliation, the relationship remains strained or lost. In a similar way, sin separates us from God. The Bible describes this separation as spiritual death. People were created to live in close relationship with God, but sin cuts us off from the very source of life.

contents.headerText: God's Plan to Restore the Relationship

contents: God did not ignore humanity's separation from Him. From the beginning, He put a plan in place to restore what was broken.

contents.headerText: The Purpose of the Old Testament Law

hiddenButton.text: What is the purpose of the Old Testament law from this passage?

revealedButton.text: The law reveals sin and shows our need for Jesus as our only hope for redemption.

contents: The law was never meant to save people by acts of obedience. It exposes humanity's inability to meet God's standard and directs attention to the need for a Savior.
These terms help explain how God restores the relationship:
To be declared righteous by God, not because of works, but through faith in Jesus. This declaration removes the guilt and penalty of sin, restoring a right relationship with God.

The Old Testament law, comprising religious, civil, and relational regulations (including but not limited to the 10 commandments), guided the Israelites' relationship with God. By obeying these laws, the Israelites demonstrated their love for both God and their neighbors. The Old Testament law today can help Christians gain insight into God's character and recognize our need for Jesus.
The state of being morally right and just before God. It is not something that can be earned or achieved through human effort, but rather a gift from God that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.
God's act of rescuing people from sin and its consequences through the death and resurrection of Jesus. It signifies forgiveness, restoration, and reconciliation with God.

The solid gold lid that covered the Ark of the Covenant. In the Old Testament it functioned as the place where God's presence dwelt and where atonement was made for the sins of the Israelites. Jesus Christ's death on the cross fulfilled the Old Testament symbolism of the mercy seat, where the High Priest would sprinkle the blood of a sacrificed animal to atone for the sins of the people. Through His sacrificial death, Jesus became the perfect and eternal sacrifice, allowing God to extend mercy and forgiveness to humanity without compromising His righteousness. Unlike the Old Testament system, where only the High Priest could approach the mercy seat once a year, Jesus' sacrifice opened the way for all people to approach God directly through faith. Therefore, Jesus Christ, as the mercy seat, is the focal point of God's redemptive plan, providing the only way for humanity to be reconciled to God and experience His abundant grace and forgiveness.

contents: Scripture is not merely informational. It is God communicating with people through human language.

When I first started playing guitar, I had to concentrate on every detail, finger placement, chords, timing. It was all about learning information. But over time, through repetition, it became muscle memory. I didn't have to think about every movement. I could listen, respond, and actually make music.
In a similar way, Scripture is more than information to master. As we grow in it, we begin to recognize God's voice and respond to Him. It moves from something we study to someone we listen to.

contents: When you see the word meditate in the Old Testament it is the Hebrew word "Hagad" which means "to moan, growl, or make a noise." This is not silent contemplative stuff we're talking about here. Rabbi Samson Hirsh explains that "hagad is that active thinking which demands expression." So Biblical meditation means that you think about what you read and as you think about it you share what you are learning with others.

All areas of your life are marked by these truths.

contents: Under the Old Covenant, the Hebrew word kaphar in Leviticus 16:17 means "to cover." Sin was addressed temporarily, not removed. Under the New Covenant, Hebrews 9:11–12 uses the Greek word lutrosis, meaning redemption or release by payment of a ransom. Sin is not covered but paid for. This shift in language reflects a shift in reality. The Old Covenant is now obsolete because it has been fulfilled (Hebrews 8:13). Jesus' sacrifice removed the record of sin completely. As Hebrews 10:17 says, "Their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more." Believers have moved from death to life, not by effort, but by the finished work of Christ.

contents: Many Christians tend to approach the Holy Spirit from one of two extremes.

On one side are those who strongly emphasize the gifts of the Spirit, such as tongues or miracles. At times, this emphasis can unintentionally alienate others or make people feel pressured or uncomfortable. A former pastor of mine used to say, "The Holy Spirit exists to make you holy, not to make you weird."

On the other side are those who, often because of past experiences or perceived baggage, largely avoid the topic of the Holy Spirit altogether. This approach can become highly intellectual, where faith is discussed but the Spirit's active role in daily life is minimized.

Cru has historically sought a healthier middle ground. The Spirit is neither ignored nor sensationalized. Instead, the focus is placed on learning how to depend on the Holy Spirit in everyday life. Bill Bright, Cru's founder, was known for saying that the most important thing he could teach a Christian was how to walk in the power of the Spirit.

contents.text: Which of these two tendencies do you resonate with more, and why?

contents: Our goal here is to understand the Holy Spirit biblically and practically, without drifting toward either extreme.
The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force or influence. The Spirit is fully God and has been active from the very beginning.

contents.headerText: How Do We Respond to the Holy Spirit?

contents.text: What does it take for a healthy plant to produce fruit?

contents: Fruit is the natural result of life and health. A plant does not force fruit to grow; it produces fruit because it is rooted, nourished, and alive. In the same way, the fruit of the Spirit is the result of walking in step with the Spirit.
By contrast, Scripture speaks of "deeds of the flesh." Deeds begin with temptation and involve choice. Sin follows a familiar pattern:
Temptation
Mental agreement
Action
Temporary gratification
Guilt
Shame
Hiding
Self-condemnation
Confession
Repentance
Restoration

Not every step must happen. At any point, repentance can interrupt the spiral. The longer someone remains in shame and hiding, the more sin maintains its grip. Life in the Spirit invites us out of the spiral and back into freedom.

contents.text: Where do you most often notice temptation gaining momentum in your life?

contents.headerText: God's Invitation: Be Filled With the Spirit

contents.text: What do you think it means to be filled with the Spirit?

contents: In this passage, "filled" does not mean like water poured into a cup. The image is closer to wind filling a sail. The Greek word pneuma means spirit, wind, or breath. To be filled with the Spirit is to be moved and directed by Him.

The goal is not to create spiritual power, but to position ourselves to receive it. Just as a sail must be adjusted to catch the wind, our lives must be oriented toward God's purposes with openness and surrender.

contents: A practical exercise for daily dependence
Agree with God about sin and acknowledge the need for His forgiveness.

Thank God for His grace, forgiveness, and indwelling Spirit.
Choose to walk attentively, responding to the Spirit's leading.
Prayer is not meant to be complicated. It can be deep or simple, structured or spontaneous, emotional or quiet. At its core, prayer is conversation with God.

People pray in many different ways. Some keep prayer lists to stay focused and remember specific needs. Others use simple frameworks like A.C.T.S. (Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving, Supplication). Some find it helpful to read written prayers from Scripture, tradition, or trusted voices in the faith. Personally, I often journal my prayers. Writing helps untangle my thoughts and gives me something to return to later, where I can see how God has been faithful over time.

The point is not finding the "right" method. There is no formula to master and no perfect wording required. God already knows your heart. Prayer is not performance; it is relationship. God invites honesty. Doubt, frustration, silence, gratitude, and praise all belong in prayer.

segments.text: Just as conversations with people take many forms, so do conversations with God. Sometimes prayer is a deep heart-to-heart. Other times it is brief, informal, or even messy. Real relationships are not one-dimensional, and prayer does not need to look the same every day. God is far more concerned

contents: Prayer is not about saying the perfect words or following the perfect method. At its core, prayer is ongoing relationship with God. Scripture presents prayer as honest conversation, dependence, worship, confession, and participation in what God is doing.

God invites us to bring real needs, real emotions, and real questions to Him. Sometimes prayer changes our circumstances. Sometimes it changes us. Sometimes the answer is clear, and sometimes it is confusing or delayed. But throughout Scripture, prayer consistently draws people deeper into trust, surrender, and intimacy with God.
Prayer is not primarily about getting everything we want from God. It is about learning to live with God.
Scripture gives us guidance without turning prayer into a rigid system.

contents: When Jesus' disciples asked how to pray, He gave them a model, not a script.
Praise God for who He is and honor His holiness.
Align your desires with God's purposes and submit to His will.
Bring daily needs honestly before God.
Confess sin and extend forgiveness to others.
Ask for strength, guidance, and protection from temptation.

contents.text: What is one simple step you could take this week to grow in prayer?

contents.subheaderText: A tool for finding the right next step of intentionality with people in your life.

contents.headerText: Identify who God may be putting in front of you
contents: You don't have to look far. The people you already see regularly are often the best place to start.
Maybe someone who lives down the hall, someone you sit next to in class, a coworker at your campus job, or someone you see at the gym or dining hall.

altButtons.text:
Write down 2–3 names
Choose one person to be intentional with this week

contents.headerText: Pay attention to the people around you
contents: It's easy to move through campus focused on your schedule and miss the people around you.
Think about walking to class, sitting before a lecture starts, waiting in line for coffee, or studying in common areas.

altButtons.text:
Put your phone away in one setting this week
Start one simple conversation “How's your week going?”

contents: Most relationships stay shallow because no one takes the first step deeper.
Instead of just talking about classes, sports, or weekend plans, you could ask about their major choice, family, goals, or what's been stressful lately.

altButtons.text:
Ask one deeper question this week
Share something a little more personal about yourself

contents: Relationships grow through time together, not just passing conversations.
This could look like grabbing coffee between classes, lunch at the dining hall, or studying together.

altButtons.text:
Invite them to coffee or a meal
Follow up if they don't give a clear answer

contents: You don't need to create something new. Just include them in what you're already doing.
Maybe you're going to a campus event, intramural game, club meeting, church gathering, or just heading to the gym.

altButtons.text:
Text them next time you're going to something
Make it casual and easy to say yes to

contents: Saying yes to their invitations builds trust and shows you care about what they care about.
This could be going to a club meeting they're part of, a game they're watching, an open mic night, or hanging out with their friend group.

altButtons.text:
Say yes to one invitation this week
Ask what they enjoy doing and join them

contents.headerText: Open the door to spiritual conversations
contents: You don't have to force it. Small steps can naturally introduce spiritual topics.
This might be when they share something stressful, talk about family, or mention something meaningful going on in their life.

altButtons.text:
Ask, “How can I pray for you?”
Follow up later and ask how things are going

contents: One long hangout is great, but consistent time together builds stronger relationships.
Think weekly meals, regular study sessions, or quick check-ins between classes.

altButtons.text:
Plan one consistent touchpoint each week
Send a quick text to stay connected

contents: Talking about your faith doesn't have to feel forced. It can come up naturally as part of your life.
You might mention something from church, a conversation from Bible study, or something you've been thinking about spiritually.

altButtons.text:
Share one personal faith-related thought
Mention a spiritual activity you're part of

contents: Before sharing what you believe, take time to understand their story.
They may have grown up in church, another religion, or with no spiritual background at all.

altButtons.text:
Ask, “Did you grow up around church or faith at all?”
Listen without correcting

contents: People often have evolving or mixed beliefs.
They might say they're spiritual, unsure, skeptical, or just haven't thought about it much.

altButtons.text:
Ask, “What do you believe about God?”
Ask follow-up questions to understand

contents.headerText: Invite them to experience Christian community
contents: Seeing faith lived out in community can be powerful.
This could be a campus ministry gathering, church service, small group, or special event.

altButtons.text:
Invite them to something you already attend
Sit with them and talk about it afterward

contents: At some point, it's important to clearly explain who Jesus is and what He has done.
This might come up during a deeper conversation, after they ask questions, or when talking about purpose, sin, or forgiveness.

altButtons.text:
Share a simple version of the gospel
Ask what they think about it

contents: Doubts are normal and often take time to work through.
They may struggle with things like suffering, hypocrisy in the church, science, or past experiences.

altButtons.text:
Ask, “What makes that hard to believe?”
Keep the conversation going over time

contents.headerText: Keep growing in your ability to share
contents: You don't need to have all the answers, but you can keep learning.
This could look like learning how to explain the gospel clearly or thinking through common questions.

altButtons.text:
Look up one question you didn't know how to answer
Ask a mentor or leader for help

contents: New faith needs structure to grow.
This could be reading the Bible together, praying, or talking through questions regularly.

altButtons.text:
Set a weekly time to meet
Start reading a short passage together

contents: Growth happens best in intentional relationships.
This could be meeting one-on-one or in a small group to learn how to follow Jesus.

altButtons.text:
Ask if they want to meet regularly
Start simple and be consistent

contents: They need more than just you to grow long-term.
This could be your friend group, a small group, or a campus ministry.

altButtons.text:
Introduce them to other believers
Bring them into group settings

contents.headerText: Plug them into a Bible study
contents: Learning alongside others helps reinforce truth and build friendships.
This might be a dorm Bible study, campus ministry group, or church small group.

altButtons.text:
Invite them to your group
Help them find one that fits

contents: Growth deepens when they begin living it out themselves.
They could start inviting friends, sharing their story, or joining you in investing in someone else.

altButtons.text:
Bring them along as you meet with someone
Encourage them to take one step with a friend
